content: Ammonium ferric citrate is a food additive identified by the E number E381 and is primarily used as an acidity regulator. It appears as either a green or reddish-brown powder, both of which are highly soluble in water. The molecular formula of ammonium iron(III) citrate is not fixed and varies depending on its preparation. It is synthesized by combining ferric hydroxide (Fe(OH)3) with an aqueous solution of citric acid and ammonia. The brown form of ammonium ferric citrate typically contains approximately 9% ammonia (NH3), 16.5–18.5% iron (Fe), and 65% hydrated citric acid. In contrast, the green form contains about 7.5% ammonia, 14.5–16% iron, and 75% hydrated citric acid. The green variant is more susceptible to reduction by light compared to the brown form. Beyond its role as a food additive, ammonium ferric citrate has several other applications. It is used in water purification processes and in the production of cyanotype prints, where it acts as a reducing agent for metal salts with low activity, such as gold and silver. In cyanotype printing, it is often combined with potassium ferricyanide to create the characteristic blue prints. In microbiology, ammonium ferric citrate is utilized in Kligler iron agar to detect hydrogen sulfide production during microbial metabolism. It is also an ingredient in the Scottish carbonated beverage Irn-Bru. In the field of medicine, ammonium ferric citrate serves as a contrast agent for imaging studies and is also employed as a hematinic, a substance used to treat or prevent iron-deficiency anemia. Ammonium ferric citrate is listed in Martindale: The Extra Pharmacopoeia, a comprehensive reference for pharmaceutical substances.
